docs.title: Writing Tests
docs.text:
This page walks through creating a test from scratch and explains the standard 7-step execution pattern used across all Intel® ESQ tests.

Tests can live in the esq extension package or in any custom extension package that builds on the sysagent core framework. Both follow identical structure and conventions — only the package path differs. See Framework Architecture for an overview of the dual-package design.

docs.title: Test Types and Required Files
docs.text:
A single test function is reused across three suite types. The suite type is defined entirely by the profile, not by the test code. Each type maps to a different report section:

Suite type Report section Purpose Pass/fail on KPIs Horizontal Horizontals (data collection) General benchmarking and metric collection No Vertical Verticals Industry-specific proxy workloads No Qualification Qualifications Validate metrics against Intel targets Yes

Because the type is profile-driven, a test does not need every file. Create only what the suite type requires:

File Horizontal Vertical Qualification Purpose test_<name>.py Required Required Required Test implementation Profile YAML Required Required Required Test parameters, devices, and (for qualification) KPI references config.yml Optional Optional Required Shared KPI definitions only

Key rules:

  • config.yml holds KPI definitions only. It defines the metric name, unit, operator, reference value, and severity for each KPI. It is the single source of truth for thresholds shared across profiles.
  • Do not put test parameters in config.yml. Parameters such as test_id, display_name, devices, timeout, and per-test requirements belong in the profile YAML. Duplicating them in config.yml creates two places to maintain and leads to drift.
  • Data-collection suites (horizontal and vertical) usually skip config.yml. They collect metrics without pass/fail validation, so no KPI definitions are needed. Mark the metrics you want highlighted with key_metrics in the profile instead.
  • Qualification profiles reuse the shared definitions. A qualification references KPIs by name with kpi_refs and refines only what differs (for example the threshold) with kpi_override. The base definition stays in config.yml.
  • Each result must have exactly one key metric. Call result.set_key_metric("metric_name") after populating result.metrics to designate the single most representative value. This is the value surfaced in summary views and used as the primary comparison point. A result with no key metric, or multiple key metrics, produces incomplete reports.
  • Prerequisite guards must fail, not skip, in qualification profiles. When a test cannot run because a required tool, capability, or kernel setting is absent, call pytest.fail for qualification profiles and pytest.skip for data-collection profiles. Use (pytest.fail if is_qualification else pytest.skip)(reason) so the same guard works correctly in both contexts. A silent skip in a qualification run hides a real system deficiency.
  • Do not add test_id or display_name to result.parameters. These are already encoded in result.name (set as f"{test_id} - {test_display_name}") and are auto-populated by the framework. Use result.parameters for domain-specific context that aids debugging — for example the device list, model name, codec, or resolution.

docs.title: Test ID and Domain Naming Convention
docs.text:
Every test parameter set carries a test_id that uniquely identifies it in reports. Use a consistent, hierarchical format so tests are easy to group, search, and trace.

Format: <MAIN>-<SUB>-<NNN>

Segment Length Meaning Examples MAIN 3 characters Main domain VSN (vision), MEM (memory), MDA (media), NET (network) SUB 3 characters Sub-domain within the main domain OBM (OpenVINO™ benchmark), STR (STREAM), DEC (decode) NNN 3 digits Sequential number within the sub-domain 001, 002, 003

Examples from the existing suites:

VSN-OBM-001    # Vision → OpenVINO benchmark → test 1
MEM-STR-001    # Memory → STREAM → test 1
MDA-DEC-004    # Media → Decode → test 4
NET-CON-002    # Network → Connectivity → test 2

Guidelines:

  • Keep MAIN and SUB to three characters where practical. Use the shortest clear abbreviation when a concept does not fit neatly (for example SNG-CPU-001 for a stress-ng CPU test).
  • Qualification profiles use a prefix that reflects the qualification (for example AES-GEN-001 for the AI Edge System generative AI test).
  • The same test_id may repeat across tiers in a qualification profile when the same test runs with tier-specific parameters. The tier distinguishes the runs.
  • Numbers are sequential and stable — do not renumber existing tests when adding new ones; append the next available number.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Test File
docs.text:
Create a test file in the suite directory of your target extension package. Add config.yml only when the test needs KPI validation (qualification). Data-collection suites can omit it:

# In the ESQ extension package:
src/esq/suites/
└── my_domain/
    └── my_feature/
        ├── config.yml          # KPI definitions — required for qualification only
        └── test_my_feature.py  # Test implementation — always required

# In a custom extension package:
src/your_package/suites/
└── my_domain/
    └── my_feature/
        ├── config.yml          # KPI definitions — required for qualification only
        └── test_my_feature.py  # Test implementation — always required

docs.title: Step 2: Test Function Overview
docs.text:
Every test function follows the same 7-step structure. The table below summarises each step and what it produces:

Step Purpose Required 1. Extract parameters Read test_id, display_name, devices, timeout from configs Always 2. Validate system requirements Skip the test if the hardware or software requirements are not met Always 3. Prepare assets Download models, videos, and build Docker* images; skipped when already cached When test needs assets 4. Execute and cache Run the test logic; return cached result on repeat runs Always 5. Validate KPIs Compare metrics against thresholds; only active when kpi_refs is set Qualification only 6. Summarize Write JSON summary and attach results to the Allure report Always 7. Surface outcome Call pytest.fail(...) on failure or interrupt so pytest records the result cleanly Always

For the complete, production-ready implementation with failure and interrupt handling, see the Test Execution Pattern section below. Use that as the base for any new test.

docs.title: Step 3: Create the Configuration File
docs.text:
This file is only required for qualification tests. It defines shared KPI thresholds and nothing else. Data-collection suites (horizontal and vertical) can skip it entirely.

Keep test parameters out of config.yml — test_id, display_name, devices, timeout, and requirements all live in the profile YAML (Step 4). Defining them here as well creates two sources of truth that drift apart over time.

# src/<package>/suites/my_domain/my_feature/config.yml
# (e.g., src/esq/suites/my_domain/my_feature/config.yml)
# Copyright (C) 2026 Intel Corporation
# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0

# KPI definitions only. Thresholds are disabled by default so the same
# definitions can be reused by data-collection suites (metrics collected,
# not enforced). Qualification profiles enable and refine them per test via
# kpi_refs + kpi_override.
kpi:
  inference_time:
    name: "Inference Time"
    type: "numeric"
    validation:
      operator: "lte"   # less than or equal
      reference: 0.5    # 500 ms max
      enabled: false    # enabled per-profile via kpi_override
    unit: "seconds"
    severity: "major"
    description: "Time taken for model inference"
    default_value: 999.0

  accuracy:
    name: "Model Accuracy"
    type: "numeric"
    validation:
      operator: "gte"   # greater than or equal
      reference: 0.90   # 90% minimum
      enabled: false    # enabled per-profile via kpi_override
    unit: "percentage"
    severity: "critical"
    description: "Model prediction accuracy"
    default_value: 0.0

docs.title: Step 4: Create a Profile
docs.text:
The profile is where all test parameters live. It sets test_id, display_name, devices, timeout, and requirements. For a qualification profile, it also references the shared KPIs with kpi_refs and refines thresholds with kpi_override.

# src/<package>/configs/profiles/horizontals/my_feature.yml
# (e.g., src/esq/configs/profiles/horizontals/my_feature.yml)
# Copyright (C) 2026 Intel Corporation
# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0

name: "profile.horizontal.my_feature"
description: "My Feature Test Suite"
params:
  labels:
    profile_group_name: "My Feature"
    profile_display_name: "My Feature - Basic Checks"
    type: "horizontal"
  requirements:
    cpu_min_cores: 4
    memory_min_gib: 8.0
    storage_min_gib: 5.0
    os_type:
      - "linux"
    docker_required: false

suites:
  - name: "my_domain"
    sub_suites:
      - name: "my_feature"
        tests:
          test_my_feature:
            params:
              # Data-collection entry: metrics collected, no pass/fail.
              # Highlight metrics with key_metrics; no kpi_refs needed.
              - test_id: "MYF-FEA-001"
                display_name: "My Feature Test - CPU"
                devices: [cpu]
                timeout: 300
                key_metrics:
                  - inference_time
                  - accuracy

              - test_id: "MYF-FEA-002"
                display_name: "My Feature Test - GPU"
                devices: [igpu]
                timeout: 300
                key_metrics:
                  - inference_time
                requirements:
                  igpu_required: true

For a qualification profile, the same test function and the same KPI definitions are reused. Add kpi_refs to enforce specific KPIs and kpi_override to enable and tune the threshold:

# src/<package>/configs/profiles/qualifications/my_feature_qual.yml
tests:
  test_my_feature:
    params:
      - test_id: "MYF-FEA-001"
        display_name: "My Feature Test - CPU"
        devices: [cpu]
        timeout: 300
        kpi_refs:
          - inference_time
          - accuracy
        kpi_override:
          inference_time:
            validation:
              reference: 0.3   # tighten to 300 ms for this qualification
              enabled: true
          accuracy:
            validation:
              enabled: true    # enable using the base 0.90 threshold

docs.title: Optional: Runtime Parameter Overrides via Environment Variables
docs.text: Some tests support overriding profile parameters at runtime through environment variables. This lets you tune a single parameter — for example, run duration or allocation size — without editing any profile file. This is useful for quick iteration, CI customization, or hardware-specific tuning.

docs.title: Naming convention
docs.text:
All runtime override variables follow this format:

ENV_SUITE_<TEST_FILENAME>_<PARAMETER>
Segment Meaning Example ENV_SUITE_ Fixed prefix distinguishing suite-level overrides — <TEST_FILENAME> Test file name without test_ and .py, uppercased; - replaced with _ test_stress_ng.py → STRESS_NG <PARAMETER> Parameter name in uppercase DURATION_SECONDS

docs.title: When to implement this
docs.text:
Add an env override only when:

  • The parameter directly controls test duration or allocation size — values that users commonly need to reduce for faster iteration
  • Users may need to adjust it per-system without editing profiles

Warning

Do not add overrides for parameters that affect result validity, such as thresholds, device selection, or test logic flags. These variables are for development and advanced testing only — setting them during a qualification run invalidates the results.

docs.title: Implementation pattern
docs.text:
# Module-level constant — single source of truth for the var name
_DURATION_ENV_VAR = "ENV_SUITE_MY_TEST_DURATION_SECONDS"

def _resolve_my_duration(configs: dict) -> int:
    """Resolve test duration, honouring the per-suite env override.

    Priority: ENV_SUITE_MY_TEST_DURATION_SECONDS env var > profile
    ``my_duration_seconds`` param > 60 default. Invalid overrides are
    ignored with a warning.
    """
    default = max(int(configs.get("my_duration_seconds", 60)), 1)

    raw_override = os.environ.get(_DURATION_ENV_VAR)
    if raw_override is None:
        return default

    try:
        override = max(int(raw_override), 1)
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        logger.warning(
            "Ignoring non-integer %s=%r; using profile default %s",
            _DURATION_ENV_VAR, raw_override, default,
        )
        return default

    logger.info("Duration override from %s: %ss", _DURATION_ENV_VAR, override)
    return override

Write the resolved value back into configs before calling execute_test_with_cache so that runs with different override values are cached independently:

duration = _resolve_my_duration(configs)
configs["my_duration_seconds"] = duration  # isolate cache key per override value

results = execute_test_with_cache(
    cached_result=cached_result,
    cache_result=cache_result,
    run_test_func=lambda: _execute_logic(duration, ...),
    test_name=test_name,
    configs=configs,
)

For the complete list of env vars supported by built-in suites, see Runtime Environment Overrides.

docs.title: Step 5: Run Your Test
docs.text:
# List available profiles
esq list

# Run your profile
esq -v run --profile profile.horizontal.my_feature

# Run a specific test using a filter
esq -d run --profile profile.horizontal.my_feature --filter test_id=MYF-FEA-001

# Run without cache (force fresh execution)
esq -d run -nc --profile profile.horizontal.my_feature

# Override a runtime parameter for this run only
ENV_SUITE_MY_TEST_DURATION_SECONDS=60 esq -v run --profile profile.horizontal.my_feature

docs.title: Test Execution Pattern
docs.text:
All Intel® ESQ tests follow a standardized 7-step pattern for consistency and reliability. Production tests wrap execution in try / except / finally so that:

  • a failed test ends with pytest.fail(...) and a clear message,
  • an interrupt (Ctrl+C) is surfaced as a proper outcome instead of a broken run,
  • validation and summarization is always running so that partial results are still reported,
  • cleanup always runs, even on failure.

Use the example shown below as the base structure for any new test.

docs.title: Full Pattern Example
docs.text:
import logging

import pytest

from sysagent.utils.core import Metrics, Result

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


def test_example(
    request,
    configs,
    cached_result,
    cache_result,
    get_kpi_config,
    validate_test_results,
    summarize_test_results,
    validate_system_requirements_from_configs,
    execute_test_with_cache,
    prepare_test,
):
    """Standard test pattern with failure and interrupt handling."""

    # ================================================================
    # STEP 1: Extract Parameters
    # ================================================================
    test_name = request.node.name.split("[")[0]
    test_id = configs.get("test_id", test_name)
    test_display_name = configs.get("display_name", test_name)
    timeout = configs.get("timeout", 300)
    devices = configs.get("devices", ["cpu"])

    # Qualification tests fail the run on interrupt; data-collection tests
    # surface it as a runtime error instead. This flag drives that decision.
    is_qualification = configs.get("labels", {}).get("type") == "qualification"

    logger.info(f"Starting test: {test_display_name}")

    # ================================================================
    # STEP 2: Validate System Requirements
    # ================================================================
    validate_system_requirements_from_configs(configs)

    # Prerequisite guards — placed after is_qualification is resolved so each
    # guard can call pytest.fail (qualification) or pytest.skip (data-collection)
    # as appropriate.  A silent skip in a qualification run hides a real system
    # deficiency; pytest.fail surfaces it clearly.
    #
    # Pattern for every prerequisite check:
    #   _outcome = pytest.fail if is_qualification else pytest.skip
    #   _outcome("reason message")
    #
    # Example — binary or capability not available:
    #   if not shutil.which("my_tool"):
    #       _outcome = pytest.fail if is_qualification else pytest.skip
    #       _outcome("my_tool not found. Install it and re-run.")

    # Outcome tracking — initialized before try block so that the final and
    # post-run blocks can always reference them.
    results = None
    test_failed = False
    test_interrupted = False
    failure_message = ""

    def cleanup():
        """Release any resources (containers, temp files, processes)."""
        # Add teardown logic here; safe to call more than once.
        pass

    try:
        # ============================================================
        # STEP 3: Prepare Assets/Dependencies
        # ============================================================
        def prepare_assets():
            return Result(
                name=f"{test_id} - Asset Preparation",
                metadata={"status": "completed"},
            )

        prepare_test(
            test_name=test_name,
            prepare_func=prepare_assets,
            configs=configs,
            name="Assets",
        )

        # ============================================================
        # STEP 4: Execute Test Logic (with caching)
        # ============================================================
        def execute_logic():
            result = Result(name=f"{test_id} - {test_display_name}")

            # Collect domain-specific metrics.
            # Every result must designate exactly ONE key metric — the most
            # representative value shown in summary views. Use set_key_metric()
            # after populating result.metrics to enforce this.
            result.metrics["throughput"] = Metrics(value=1234.5, unit="ops/sec")
            result.metrics["latency_ms"] = Metrics(value=42.0, unit="ms")
            result.set_key_metric("throughput")  # exactly one key metric per result

            # Add domain-specific parameters for the Allure report.
            # Do NOT add test_id or display_name — those are already encoded in
            # result.name and are auto-populated by the framework.
            result.parameters["Devices"] = ", ".join(devices)

            result.metadata["status"] = True
            result.update_timestamps()
            return result

        results = execute_test_with_cache(
            cached_result=cached_result,
            cache_result=cache_result,
            run_test_func=execute_logic,
            test_name=test_name,
            configs=configs,
        )

        # Mark the test as failed when the execution reports a non-passing status.
        if not results.metadata.get("status", False):
            test_failed = True
            failure_message = results.metadata.get("error", f"{test_display_name} failed")

    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        # Ctrl+C or run cancellation — record it and re-surface after cleanup.
        test_interrupted = True
        failure_message = "Interrupt detected during test execution"
        logger.error(failure_message)

    except Exception as error:
        # Any unexpected error — capture the message and continue to reporting.
        test_failed = True
        failure_message = f"Unexpected error during test execution: {error}"
        logger.error(failure_message, exc_info=True)

    finally:
        # Always release resources, even on failure or interrupt.
        cleanup()

    # ================================================================
    # Ensure a result object always exists so validation and
    # summarization can record the outcome — even when execution was
    # interrupted before producing results.
    # ================================================================
    if results is None:
        results = Result(
            name=f"{test_id} - {test_display_name}",
            metadata={"status": False},
            extended_metadata={"message": failure_message or "Test did not complete"},
            metrics={},
        )

    # ================================================================
    # STEP 5: Validate Results Against KPIs (optional)
    # Only enforced when kpi_refs are configured for the test. Wrapped so a
    # validation error never masks the underlying test outcome.
    # ================================================================
    try:
        validate_test_results(
            results=results,
            configs=configs,
            get_kpi_config=get_kpi_config,
            test_name=test_name,
        )
    except Exception as validation_error:
        logger.error(f"Validation failed: {validation_error}")

    # ================================================================
    # STEP 6: Generate Summary (always runs)
    # ================================================================
    try:
        summarize_test_results(
            results=results,
            test_name=test_name,
            configs=configs,
            get_kpi_config=get_kpi_config,
        )
    except Exception as summary_error:
        logger.error(f"Summarization failed: {summary_error}", exc_info=True)

    cache_result(results)

    logger.info(f"Test completed: {test_display_name}")

    # ================================================================
    # STEP 7: Surface the outcome
    # Report interrupts and failures as proper pytest results instead of
    # leaving a broken/errored status behind.
    # ================================================================
    if test_interrupted:
        if is_qualification:
            pytest.fail(failure_message)
        else:
            raise RuntimeError(failure_message)
    if test_failed:
        pytest.fail(failure_message)

docs.title: Execution Flow Diagram
docs.text:
1. Parameter Extraction
   ├─> Read test_id, display_name, timeout, devices
   └─> Configure logging

2. System Validation
   ├─> Check CPU / Memory / Storage
   ├─> Check device availability
   ├─> Check software dependencies and tool prerequisites
   ├─> Data-collection profile → pytest.skip when prerequisites not met
   └─> Qualification profile  → pytest.fail when prerequisites not met

3. Asset Preparation
   ├─> Download models and videos
   ├─> Build Docker* images
   └─> Set up test environment

4. Test Execution (Cached)
   ├─> Check cache for existing results
   ├─> Cache hit  → return cached results
   ├─> Cache miss → execute test logic
   └─> On error/interrupt → record message, run cleanup, continue

5. KPI Validation (optional — only when kpi_refs are configured)
   ├─> Load KPI configurations
   ├─> Compare results vs. thresholds
   └─> Mark passed / failed / skipped

6. Result Summarization (always runs)
   ├─> Generate JSON summary
   ├─> Create Allure attachments
   └─> Generate visualizations

7. Surface Outcome
   ├─> Cleanup already ran in finally
   ├─> Interrupt  → pytest.fail (qualification) / RuntimeError (collection)
   └─> Failure    → pytest.fail with failure_message

docs.title: Docker engine
docs.text:
Docker* Engine Download Source

Intel® ESQ uses download.docker.com* as the default download source. To use a custom download source*, configure it with:

export DOCKER_SOURCE_URL=<custom_docker_source_url>

Install Docker* Engine:

# Add Docker's official GPG key:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install ca-certificates curl
sudo install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings
sudo curl -fsSL ${DOCKER_SOURCE_URL:-https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu}/gpg -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc
sudo chmod a+r /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc

# Add the repository to Apt sources:
sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.sources <<EOF
Types: deb
URIs: ${DOCKER_SOURCE_URL:-https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu}
Suites: $(. /etc/os-release && echo "${UBUNTU_CODENAME:-$VERSION_CODENAME}")
Components: stable
Architectures: $(dpkg --print-architecture)
Signed-By: /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc
EOF

sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin

Add your user to the docker group:

Warning

Adding your user to the docker group grants root-level access. This should only be done on development or test systems.

sudo usermod -aG docker $USER

To activate your new group membership immediately in your current terminal, run:

newgrp docker

This command starts a new shell session with updated group permissions, allowing you to use Docker* without logging out. You can now verify Docker* installation is successful by running the hello-world image:

docker pull hello-world

Note

If you see a list of containers (even if empty), your user is correctly added to the docker group. If you get a permission error, ensure you have run newgrp docker in your terminal. For persistent access across all sessions, log out and log back in, or reboot your system.

Note

If you cannot pull the image, your network may be unable to reach the default registry. Configure a mirror registry in the Docker* daemon configuration:

sudo mkdir -p /etc/docker
sudo tee /etc/docker/daemon.json > /dev/null <<EOF
{
    "registry-mirrors": [
        "<mirror-registry-source>"
    ]
}
EOF

Additional Reference

For detailed Docker* installation instructions, see the official Docker* Engine installation documentation.

Development Version

To access the latest features that may not be available in the current release, you can install the development version from the main branch: 

uv tool install --force --refresh git+https://github.com/open-edge-platform/edge-system-qualification.git@main

Install Intel® ESQ from GitHub*:

uv tool install --force --refresh git+https://github.com/open-edge-platform/edge-system-qualification.git@main

Verify that Intel® ESQ is working correctly:

esq --version

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh && source $HOME/.local/bin/env

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
Upgrading Intel® ESQ

Before running a new version of Intel® ESQ, clean up any previously created esq_data folder to prevent leftover data from interfering with the new installation:

esq clean --all

Verbose Output

Use --verbose to show detailed execution logs:

esq --verbose run

Driver Requirements and Hardware Changes

Intel® GPU and NPU tests require specific drivers. Ensure you have the latest Intel® drivers installed for your hardware configuration. If you run tests on different hardware or swap system components, clean up the cache before rerunning tests:

esq --verbose clean --cache-only

Download Source

Intel® ESQ uses HuggingFace* as the default download source. For ModelScope*, configure it with:

export PREFER_MODELSCOPE=1

Run the advanced setup script to enable full test coverage:

sudo bash -c "$(wget -qLO - https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open-edge-platform/edge-system-qualification/refs/heads/main/scripts/system-setup-advanced.sh)"

Re-run after reboot

All changes applied by system-setup-advanced.sh are in current session only and resets automatically after reboot. Re-run the script after each reboot before executing tests that depend on it.

Advanced setup modules:

Module What it changes Locked Memory Limit Sets RLIMIT_MEMLOCK to unlimited for the current session so memtester can lock all available RAM pages. Without this, memory-related tests will be limited or fail

docs.title: System setup rt
docs.text:
For RT latency tests, run the RT setup script:

sudo bash -c "$(wget -qLO - https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open-edge-platform/edge-system-qualification/refs/heads/main/scripts/system-setup-rt.sh)"

Re-run after reboot

All changes applied by system-setup-rt.sh are in current session only and resets automatically after reboot. Re-run after each reboot before executing RT tests.

RT setup modules:

Module What it changes Real-Time Latency Tools Copies cyclictest and chrt with cap_sys_nice and cap_ipc_lock capabilities to a session tmpfs so RT latency tests run at SCHED_FIFO priority without sudo. Cleared on reboot MSR Tools Copies rdmsr and wrmsr with cap_sys_rawio to the same session tmpfs for Intel® RDT/CAT partition reporting and L3 CAT write verification. Cleared on reboot Kernel Tuning Grants world-write on cpuidle sysfs disable files (C-state control); disables timer migration (/proc/sys/kernel/timer_migration=0); sets up a session tee with cap_sys_admin for non-root cpuidle writes. Cleared on reboot

Feature Availability

Some features configured by this script are optional. Intel® ESQ will still run if skipped, but certain metrics and capabilities may be unavailable.

Test suite test_chatqna_core (src/esq/suites/ai/gen/test_chatqna_core.py) Integration type Type 2: reproduce the original flow. It runs the application's own Docker Compose stack and configuration from open-edge-platform/edge-ai-libraries, pinned to a commit. docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Download the application's compose file, NGINX template, and model configuration from edge-ai-libraries at assets_repo_ref, and bind every published port to 127.0.0.1.

  3. Ingest the documents of corpus_dir, then send the prompts of prompt_file (up to prompt_limit).
  4. Report startup time, ingestion time, p50 and p95 query latency, time to first token, and the query success rate. A scenario_matrix entry runs several backends in one test case and reports them together.

docs.title: DL Streamer Pipeline
docs.text:
Runs an Intel® DL Streamer pipeline in Docker containers and finds the largest number of concurrent video streams that keep the target frame rate on each device.

Test suite test_dlstreamer (src/esq/suites/ai/vision/test_dlstreamer.py) Integration type Type 1: generic suite. The pipeline, models, and videos come from the profile. Key metric streams_max (streams), per device as streams_max_<device> Devices CPU, iGPU, dGPU, NPU, or several stages on different devices

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Download the profile's assets (videos and models) and build the analyzer images.
  2. Run a baseline on each device to estimate how many streams it can carry.
  3. Search for the highest stream count whose per-stream FPS stays at or above target_fps, starting from the baseline.
  4. Run all qualified devices together and report the total and per-device streams_max.

docs.title: VLM Prompt
docs.text:
Sends prompts with images or video frames to a vision language model (VLM) on OpenVINO™ Model Server (OVMS) and measures token throughput, request latency, and how many requests the device can serve at the same time within a latency target.

Test suite test_vlm_prompt (src/esq/suites/ai/gen/test_vlm_prompt.py) Integration type Type 1: generic suite. The model, prompt, and media come from the profile. Key metric Fixed load: output_token_throughput (tokens/sec). Stream density: streams_max (streams). Both per device, for example output_token_throughput_igpu or streams_max_dgpu1. Devices CPU, iGPU, dGPU. A category that matches several devices (two dGPUs) runs once on each.

It is the baseline of the Order Accuracy applications: only the model server and a load generator run, without the application's other services. The Order Accuracy suites (Type 2) run the full applications.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Export the model with the OVMS export flow of the text generation suite (or download a pre-quantized model), write the serving graph, and download the media.
  2. Start one OVMS container on the device.
  3. Run the load generator (src/vlm_prompt/vlm_client.py) in its own uv venv. It sends chat-completion requests from concurrent workers and records latency and token usage of every request.
  4. Report the results:
    • Fixed load (benchmark_mode: fixed_workers): benchmark_workers run for benchmark_duration. Requests started during benchmark_init_duration are left out.
    • Stream density (benchmark_mode: stream_density): adds concurrent requests until the latency exceeds target_latency_ms and reports the largest count that passed. The count is searched with the latency-guided search of test_dlstreamer (density_search: adaptive) or one step at a time (linear).

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Per device, with the device as suffix (_cpu, _igpu, _dgpu1):

Metric Unit Meaning output_token_throughput tokens/sec Standard aggregate throughput of the system: the generated tokens of all measured requests, from all concurrent workers, divided by the measurement window from the start of the first request to the end of the last (key metric of fixed load) request_latency_avg sec Mean duration of a full request streams_max streams Stream density: most concurrent requests within the target (key metric of stream density) time_to_first_token_cold_start sec Time to first token of the first request after the model server starts time_to_first_token_warm_start sec Mean time to first token of the following requests

output_token_throughput is a system-level value over many requests, not the rate of one request. With one worker it is the rate of requests that follow each other. With several workers it adds up their tokens, so it grows with the concurrency until the device is saturated. It is not the mean of the per-request rates, which is the throughput_mean_sec of the Order Accuracy applications, see Metric Naming.

The metadata of the result also has request_count, measurement_window_sec, input_sequence_length_avg, output_sequence_length_avg (in tokens), and throughput_mean_sec, see below.

docs.title: Metric Naming
docs.text:
The names follow the LLM serving metrics of NVIDIA GenAI-Perf and AIPerf and the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions, written in snake case with sec for seconds. The suite does not use the names of the Order Accuracy applications, so it can serve other workloads.

ESQ metric AIPerf, GenAI-Perf OpenTelemetry GenAI Take-Away and Dine-In applications request_latency_avg request_latency (mean) gen_ai.client.inference.duration vlm_avg_call_duration of test_ta_vlm and test_di_vlm, VLM_AVERAGE_CALL_DURATION in consolidated_metrics.csv, elapsed_sec of the ovms_vlm_request event output_token_throughput output_token_throughput (same definition, aggregate of all concurrent requests) None None. The closest is throughput_mean_sec, which is a per-request mean, see the note below time_to_first_token_cold_start, time_to_first_token_warm_start time_to_first_token gen_ai.server.time_to_first_token Not reported input_sequence_length_avg, output_sequence_length_avg input_sequence_length, output_sequence_length gen_ai.client.inference.operation.input_tokens, ...output_tokens prompt_tokens, completion_tokens of the ovms_vlm_request event, generated_tokens streams_max None None Result of make benchmark-stream-density

throughput_mean_sec of the applications is the mean over the requests of the generated tokens divided by the request latency. It has no standard name, and it is not the standard output token throughput, which divides all generated tokens by the measurement window and so also counts the time between requests. The two are equal when requests follow each other without a gap, and differ by the time the client needs to prepare a request (0.3% for Dine-In, 7.6% for Take-Away, which prepares 3 video frames per request on the CPU). The suite keeps the application value as throughput_mean_sec in the metadata, and the comparison uses it. The applications have no time per output token in the standard sense: their tpot_sec is the request latency divided by the generated tokens, which includes the time to first token.

The time to first token follows the name and unit of gen_ai.server.time_to_first_token in the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions, called TTFT in MLPerf Inference. It covers the time in the queue and the prefill of the prompt and images. It is measured by a short probe of ttft_requests streaming requests, one after another, right after the server starts and before any other request. The benchmark requests stay non-streaming like the source applications, so the throughput and latency are unchanged. The cold start is the first request, which pays for the lazy initialization of the model, and the warm start is the mean of the others. Requests repeat the same prompt and media, so the warm start benefits from prefix caching like the benchmark requests do. With restart_server_per_iteration the probe runs only after the first start.

docs.title: Comparison With the Upstream Benchmarks
docs.text:
Measured on Intel® Core™ Ultra 9 285K with Intel® Arc™ Pro B70 (GPU.1), against the full applications (test_ta_vlm, test_di_vlm, and the upstream make benchmark-stream-density). Both send the same requests to the same model: 288 prompt and 15 completion tokens for Take-Away, 204 prompt tokens and the same answer per image for Dine-In.

Fixed load, warm requests (request_latency_avg, throughput_mean_sec per request):

Device Take-Away app Take-Away baseline Dine-In app Dine-In baseline CPU 5.04 s, 2.99 4.46 s, 3.36 (−11%) 3.10 s, 8.84 3.05 s, 8.95 (−1.6%) iGPU 5.54 s, 2.71 5.42 s, 2.78 (−2%) 3.17 s, 8.63 3.16 s, 8.66 (−0.4%) dGPU 0.375 s, 41.07 0.294 s, 50.81 (−22%) 0.400 s, 68.52 0.388 s, 70.64 (−3.1%)

The percentage is the latency of the baseline relative to the application, so a negative value means the baseline is faster. The Dine-In figures are from a later run than the Take-Away figures. The Dine-In application sends only 8 requests (the 4 images twice), so its warm value is the mean of the second pass of 4 requests. The baseline value is the mean of all requests after its warm-up. A single application run varies by a few percent: a first CPU run gave 3.66 s where the repeat gave 3.10 s.

Stream density, largest count within 10 s average latency:

Device Take-Away app Take-Away baseline Dine-In app Dine-In baseline CPU 1 2 11 12 iGPU 1 1 7 7 dGPU 50 (limit) 323 50 (limit) 380

The upstream benchmark stops after 50 steps, so it reports 50 on the dGPU. The profiles set max_workers: 600 (the default of the suite is 50), so the baseline finds the real maximum there.

What the gaps mean:

  • Dine-In matches within 3%, and the baseline is never slower, because its workers send requests back to back like the load generator and no other service runs between them.
  • Take-Away is slower in the application. On the CPU its frame selector, video decoding, OCR, and semantic matching share the cores with the model. On the GPUs the application adds about 0.1 s per request, which is large for a 0.3 s dGPU request.
  • Take-Away stream density restarts the whole stack per step. The baseline does the same (restart_server_per_iteration) but sends each step's requests at once, while the application's stations are staggered, so its maximum is a conservative value.

Compare warm requests with warm requests: test_ta_vlm averages its cold first request into about 6 calls, and test_di_vlm averages the cold requests of its first pass into 8 calls (4.39 s on the CPU against 3.10 s warm), so their reported throughput_mean_sec is lower than their own warm requests.

docs.title: Checking Comparability
docs.text:
When a profile reproduces another application, check the ingredients in this order:

  1. Prompt and media: the same usage.prompt_tokens as the application's metrics log.
  2. Model: the same nncf section in openvino_language_model.xml and the same .bin sizes. A pre-quantized model with the same name is often different (for example OpenVINO/MiniCPM-V-4_5-int4-cw-ov is channel-wise symmetric INT4).
  3. Serving: the same OVMS image and LLMCalculatorOptions in graph.pbtxt.
  4. Metrics: warm requests on both sides.

docs.title: REST Workers and max_num_seqs
docs.text:
• rest_workers is the number of requests OVMS works on at once. On the dGPU, with more clients than workers, throughput followed the workers: 2.7, 6.8, 12.3, and 13.1 requests/s with 2, 4, 8, and the default (24) workers. Keep it at least as high as the concurrency the test needs. With 4, Dine-In stream density on the dGPU drops from 380 to 126.
  • max_rest_workers is a failsafe. Each worker needs about 3 file descriptors, so the default on a 344-core system (1032) exceeds the usual limit of 1024 and OVMS fails with Too many open files. The profiles set 128. The value in use is shown as OVMS REST Workers in the result.
  • max_num_seqs did not limit these workloads. Raising it from 4 to 16 changed throughput by less than 6% on the dGPU and iGPU. Keep the application's value (4).

docs.title: Real-Time Wakeup Latency (cyclictest)
docs.text:
Measures the worst-case wakeup latency of real-time threads with cyclictest on isolated CPU cores, while stress-ng loads the other cores. Optional cache partitioning and C-state settings show the effect of real-time tuning.

Test suite test_cyclictest (src/esq/suites/realtime/performance/test_cyclictest.py) Integration type Type 1: generic suite. It wraps cyclictest and stress-ng, and the profile sets the cores, timing, load, and tuning. Key metric max_latency_us (µs, lower is better), with avg_latency_us and min_latency_us Devices CPU

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Optionally partition the L3 cache with Intel® Cache Allocation Technology (cat_enabled) and disable deep C-states on the real-time cores (cstate_disable_enabled). The previous state is saved.
  2. Start stress-ng on the stress cores.
  3. Run cyclictest on the real-time cores for cyclic_duration.
  4. Report the latencies and restore the saved state, also when the test is interrupted.

The optimizations need the modules of scripts/system-setup-rt.sh.

docs.title: CPU
docs.text:
Identifies the CPU (brand, processor number, generation, codename, segment) and reports its socket count, core counts, and frequencies. Optionally checks the CPU against a list of qualified generations or SKUs.

Test suite test_cpu (src/esq/suites/system/cpu/test_cpu.py) Integration type Type 1: generic suite. ESQ checks the system directly, and the profile selects the checks. Key metric Only the metrics listed in kpi_refs or key_metrics: cpu_compatibility (1 pass, 0 fail), sockets, physical_cores, logical_cores (cores), max_frequency_mhz, min_frequency_mhz (MHz) Devices CPU

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Read the CPU details from the system information cache. The processor number is the last token of the brand string (for example 285K).
  2. Run the compatibility check. The allowlists (processor_numbers, exact_generations, supported_generations) are combined with OR: the CPU passes if it matches any of them. unsupported_generations is used only when no allowlist is set. With no list set, cpu_compatibility is 1 (audit mode).
  3. Keep only the metrics named in kpi_refs or key_metrics. Brand, generation, codename, segment, and check mode are recorded as parameters.
  4. Validate the KPIs. Thresholds are disabled by default and enabled per profile with kpi_override.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Description processor_numbers [] Allowlist of processor numbers, for example ["155H", "285K"]. Case-insensitive, whole-token match in the brand string. exact_generations [] Allowlist with exact matching. Each entry is a generation string, a dict with any of generation, codename, product_collection, segment, or a list [generation, product_collection, segment]. supported_generations [] Allowlist that also accepts newer generations of the same product family unsupported_generations [] Denylist. The CPU passes if its generation is not listed and not older than a listed entry. Ignored when an allowlist is set. key_metrics [] Metrics to report (horizontal profiles) kpi_refs, kpi_override [], unset Metrics to report and validate, and their thresholds (qualification profiles), see KPI Validation

docs.text:
Runs OpenVINO™ benchmark_app with a YOLO model on the GPU and records the GPU frequency, utilization, and power, and the CPU utilization and frequency, while the GPU is under load.

Test suite test_system_gpu (src/esq/suites/system/gpu/test_system_gpu.py) Integration type Type 1: generic suite. ESQ runs OpenVINO™ benchmark_app in its own container. The model, precision, device, and duration come from the profile. Key metric frequency_max_igpu or frequency_max_dgpu (GHz), for the tested device Devices iGPU, dGPU

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Download the YOLO model from Ultralytics, export it to OpenVINO™ IR, and download a test image. YOLOv5n replaces the default yolov5s on Intel Atom® and Celeron® processors.
  2. Build the test image on top of the DL Streamer image prepared by test_dlstreamer (the dGPU variant on a discrete GPU).
  3. Run the container on each device of the device category. It runs benchmark_app for duration_hrs while collecting telemetry with intel_gpu_top (and xpu-smi for dGPU power).
  4. Read averages_summary.csv and report frequency (mean on iGPU, peak on dGPU), stability (standard deviation, minimum, range), utilization, and power. Values that could not be collected are reported as -1.

docs.text: Parameter Default Description device igpu Device category to test: igpu or dgpu models, precision ["yolov5s"], FP16 YOLO model to export and its precision. Only the first model is benchmarked, and the container loads only the FP16 export. duration_hrs 0.15 Benchmark duration in hours. docs.title: Memory Health
docs.text:
Checks installed RAM for faults while the OS is running, with one of two probes: the EDAC ECC error counters, or a memtester bit-pattern test. It collects data and does not fail on the errors it finds, unless a profile enables the KPI.

Test suite test_memory_health (src/esq/suites/system/memory/test_memory_health.py) Integration type Type 1: generic suite. ESQ reads the EDAC counters or runs memtester on the host. The probe, test size, and iterations come from the profile. Key metric EDAC: uncorrectable_errors (errors). memtester: memory_errors (errors, -1 if memtester did not complete). Devices System memory

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. EDAC (check_type: edac): read the correctable and uncorrectable error counts per memory controller and DIMM from /sys/devices/system/edac/mc, and list the DIMMs with errors. Add ras-mc-ctl output when it is installed. Without EDAC the test reports edac_available: false and still passes.
  2. memtester (check_type: memtester): run memtester <size>M <iterations> on the host and count the FAILURE lines. The test fails if memtester is not installed, cannot allocate the region, or exits for another reason.
  3. Save the report to esq_data/data/suites/system/memory/results/<test_id>/.

With memtester_size_mb: auto, the size is MemAvailable minus the larger of the two reserves, capped at the locked-memory limit (ulimit -l). memtester locks every page it tests, so raise the limit (ulimit -l unlimited) to test more memory.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Description check_type edac Probe to run: edac or memtester memtester_size_mb 256 Size in MB to test. auto, dynamic, available, all, or a value of 0 or less sizes it from the available memory. memtester_dynamic_reserve_mb, memtester_dynamic_reserve_percent 512, 10.0 Memory left free in dynamic sizing. The larger of the two is used. memtester_iterations 1 memtester loops timeout 300 Seconds for the memtester run kpi_refs, kpi_override [], unset KPIs to validate and their thresholds (qualification profiles), see KPI Validation

The environment variables ENV_SUITE_MEMORY_HEALTH_MEMTESTER_SIZE_MB and ENV_SUITE_MEMORY_HEALTH_MEMTESTER_ITERATIONS override the profile values at run time.

Test suite test_ta_vlm (src/esq/suites/vertical/retail/test_ta_vlm.py), test_di_vlm (src/esq/suites/vertical/retail/test_di_vlm.py) Integration type Type 2: reproduce the original flow. docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Clone intel-retail/order-accuracy into esq_data/thirdparty/order-accuracy, check out commit_id, and run make update-submodules. Both suites share this clone.
  2. For each device, write TARGET_DEVICE into the application's .env and export the model with ovms-service/setup_models.sh. Take-Away also downloads its sample video (make download-sample-video). Dine-In uses the images and orders bundled with the repository.
  3. Run make benchmark with benchmark_workers and benchmark_duration (fixed-workers mode). The target starts the application's services.
  4. Run make consolidate-metrics, read throughput_mean_sec from vlm_performance_metrics_*.txt and VLM_AVERAGE_CALL_DURATION (vlm_avg_call_duration) from consolidated_metrics.csv, then stop the services with make down.

docs.title: Proxy Pipelines
docs.text:
Runs metro proxy pipelines (License Plate Recognition, Smart NVR, Headed Visual AI, VSaaS) with Intel® DL Streamer in a benchmark container and finds the largest number of 1080p streams that keep 30 FPS.

Test suite test_proxy_pipelines (src/esq/suites/vertical/vision/test_proxy_pipelines.py) Integration type Type 1: generic suite. ESQ's own benchmark container (src/containers/proxy_pipeline_benchmark/) runs the pipeline that the profile selects with pptest. Key metric max_streams (streams), the best result across the tested devices. Also avg_fps, gpu_freq_mhz, pkg_power_w, duration_s. Devices iGPU, dGPU. LPR can also use the NPU when the platform has one.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Download the models and videos of the selected pipeline into esq_data/data/vertical/vision/results/ppl/resources.
  2. Build the device-specific DL Streamer images (as test_dlstreamer) and the proxy pipeline image on top of the matching one (CPU/iGPU, dGPU, or NPU).
  3. Run the container with all devices of devices. Per device and model, it searches for the highest stream count that keeps the target FPS (search_algorithm) and writes a CSV file.
  4. Read max_streams from the CSV row with the most streams and avg_fps from the runner log. If the CSV already exists and force_run is false, the benchmark is skipped and the existing CSV is read.

docs.title: KVM Virtualization
docs.text:
Checks that the system can host KVM virtual machines, estimates how many VMs can get their own display, keyboard, and mouse, and measures how fast a QEMU/KVM VM reboots.

Test suite test_kvm_compatibility, test_kvm_vm_capacity, test_kvm_qemu_reboot (src/esq/suites/virtualization/kvm/) Integration type Type 1: generic suite. ESQ checks the system directly, and the profile selects the checks. Key metric Compatibility: kvm_dev_accessible (true/false), or vt_d_enabled and nested_virt_enabled when only those checks run. Capacity: peripheral_vm_capacity (vms). Reboot: avg_reboot_time (seconds). Devices Host system (CPU, IOMMU, connected displays and USB input devices) Test What it verifies test_kvm_compatibility VT-x CPU flags, VT-d/IOMMU, kvm and kvm_intel modules, VFIO modules and devices, nested virtualization, and access to /dev/kvm. Collects data only. The test always passes. test_kvm_vm_capacity Number of VMs that can each get one display, one keyboard, and one mouse by passthrough. It is the smaller of the display count and keyboard/mouse pairs, and 0 without IOMMU groups. Collects data only. Qualification profiles set a KPI on it. test_kvm_qemu_reboot One QEMU/KVM VM is created, booted, rebooted reboot_count times, and removed. Fails if any step fails.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Compatibility: read /proc/cpuinfo, the DMAR table and IOMMU groups, lsmod, the kvm_intel nested parameter, and /dev/kvm for each enabled check, and save the details under esq_data/data/suites/virtualization/kvm/results/<test_id>.
  2. Capacity: count IOMMU groups, connected displays, and keyboard/mouse pairs (pairs on one USB hub first), and attach a topology diagram and lsusb -t.
  3. Reboot: download guest_image_url (or create a blank qcow2 disk), seed an SSH key with cloud-init, and start a headless VM with the chosen firmware.
  4. Reboot: wait for the guest with guest_ready_probe, optionally read /etc/os-release over SSH, then reboot the VM and time each cycle until the guest is ready again. Image preparation is not part of the reboot times.
